searchText: my 2 cents regarding the 2nd question: people who have decided to stake have explicitly accepted that risk(and it is detailed clearly in the current launchpad flow,i expect it will probably be even more prominent come mainnet time). You def don't want to make people complacent and give the impression that a bailout would even be considered in such a scenario or you can just forget about client diversity as people will just converge on the one that has accrued the biggest traction/has the best UX and resiliency of the network be damned.Bugs happen Agreed that has been put forward quite clearly. But what is supposed to be a security of the chain mechanism finds itself being the angry guard exerting it’s anger over the condemned in such a situation. I doubt you’d be able to spin that in any way that would cast a positive public opinion The chain probably needs to have some sort of recognised infancy, where there is some sort of compensation for such issues. But it quickly becomes very difficult to argue about which products are "in" and which are "out" of the compensated entities, given the cost of audits and the pace of change of the software. The best answer is to insulate the components from each other, so that (for example) a bug in a beacon node _cannot_ create a slashable offence because it's the signer that protects against that. This would allow a reduction in the surface that needs to be protected against, and more chance of being able to provide some sort of limited set of guarantees. I still think that stakers should really be running multiple clients and validating the results are the same before attesting. Im sorry for my ignorance. But what are shakers? **vbuterin** I think in phase 0 that's not really needed because the code to prevent self-slashing is so simple **vbuterin** But in phase 1, having the validator client run a verification over eg. the eth1 state transition using a different implementation from the beacon node before signing is definitely something worth trying to do Trouble with that is that it's quite possible for the results to be different without being wrong. Client A may be behind client B in an absolute sense, but if the majority of nodes are in client A's position then that's where the vote weight goes. The actual attack surface for phase 0 is pretty small, in terms of not being slashed. There are a few simple rules that the signer has to follow. > Im sorry for my ignorance. Client A may be behind client B in an absolute sense, but if the majority of nodes are in client A's position then that's where the vote weight goes. Wouldn't you want to abstain in such a split? > **vbuterin** > I think in phase 0 that's not really needed because the code to prevent self-slashing is so simple A lot of issues will come from the operational side: users running the same validator keys on two nodes at the same time, not failing over properly, exposing their keys, _etc._ Not something that can be easily protected against, but it won't make the losses any less painful. **vbuterin** true > Wouldn't you want to abstain in such a split? <@!301186049323958275> Nope; you get paid to vote, even if bits of the vote are incorrect (the vote has three sections, at least one of which you should get right unless you're *way* behind, plus you gain more for timeliness). hey, so, i was looking at the beacon chain explorer (at beaconcha.in), and I noticed that there are epochs that are marked as not finalized that have later epochs that are marked as finalized (presumably finalized checkpoints). one example would be epoch 2240. there are also some epochs during the low participation portion of the launch of the medalla testnet (for example, epoch 3000 where participation was 2%) and yet, this is marked as finalized. is there some discrepancy/errors in how the beacon chain explorer marks epochs as finalized? or am i misunderstanding something about the beacon chain explorer? this seems like a peculiarity of the explorer and/or the API it is requesting from When epoch X is directly finalized, all epochs prior to it in the chain are then considered "finalized" even if say `X-2` wasn't directly finalized. That said, the block epxlorer could choose to note that subtlety in a few different ways. Not sure what beaconcha.in is doing exactly <@!291925846556540928> do you have an explorer that you prefer that you know also has accurate info?

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content:
The chain probably needs to have some sort of recognised infancy, where there is some sort of compensation for such issues.  But it quickly becomes very difficult to argue about which products are "in" and which are "out" of the compensated entities, given the cost of audits and the pace of change of the software.

The best answer is to insulate the components from each other, so that (for example) a bug in a beacon node _cannot_ create a slashable offence because it's the signer that protects against that.  This would allow a reduction in the surface that needs to be protected against, and more chance of being able to provide some sort of limited set of guarantees.

excerpts.author: jgm
excerpts.content:
Trouble with that is that it's quite possible for the results to be different without being wrong.  Client A may be behind client B in an absolute sense, but if the majority of nodes are in client A's position then that's where the vote weight goes.

The actual attack surface for phase 0 is pretty small, in terms of not being slashed.  There are a few simple rules that the signer has to follow.

A lot of issues will come from the operational side: users running the same validator keys on two nodes at the same time, not failing over properly, exposing their keys, _etc._  Not something that can be easily protected against, but it won't make the losses any less painful.
